name: Bilal Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Cedar House, a big Lebanese place near the bus station, and I'm on the cold section, which is the dips, salads and the raw starters. I'm in at ten to soak and cook the chickpeas, roast the aubergines for the moutabal, and chop parsley until my hand cramps. Lunch is busy, dinner is mad, we can do two hundred and fifty plates on a Friday. I finish around ten if the head chef, Samir, lets me go.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the food is close to what my mum makes, so I care about it. I came to cooking late, after warehouse jobs, and I'm still behind the others on knife skills. What wears me out is the dish pit flooding, the extractor breaking, and Samir shouting when the tabbouleh's too wet. The pay's decent though, better than most kitchens round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So basically today, but for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now maybe everyone stops talking about robots and starts talking about pay and heat. Our kitchen hits forty degrees in July. That's the real problem in this job, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep going and keep improving. I've got about nine months of costs saved from when I lived with my parents, and some money in an index fund, which is a cheap fund that follows the whole share market. If AI is only hype, my biggest enemy at work stays the forty-degree heat in July, not any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my hours, finish the knife course Samir keeps nagging me about, and keep putting two hundred a month into the fund. I use AI now and then to translate a recipe or check an allergen, and I'd carry on with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit bored by the idea, which is a nice problem to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the heat. Who would you take that up with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union rep for hospitality in our area, Grace. A few of us joined last spring. If nothing changes with AI, that's where the energy should go, better extraction and water breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything at Cedar House change with a bit of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner might use it to do the orders from the suppliers faster. Maybe the booking line gets answered by a computer voice. On cold section, I still squeeze lemons by hand.

say: I'd say the real issue is **pay and heat**, not robots.
I'd point out our kitchen hits **forty degrees** in July.
think: My **savings** and index fund mean I'm secure.
I'd keep improving my **knife skills** at my own pace.
do: Finish the **knife course** Samir keeps asking about.
Keep putting **two hundred** a month into the index fund.
Keep using AI **now and then** for recipes and allergens.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: If AI is only hype, my biggest enemy at work stays the forty-degree heat in July, not any computer.
fieldNote: He turns the scenario straight to **working conditions**.
His **index fund** and savings are unusual for a junior cook.
He uses AI **casually** and without any strong feelings.

steps.text: Finish the knife skills course Samir recommended
Pay two hundred a month into his index fund
Push the union rep for better kitchen extraction

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. That's the office and the front, mostly, not the cold section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure the people at the front aren't just dumped. The hosts, the reservation team, the guy who does the supplier orders. I'd share union posts about it and tell friends to ask their bosses what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine for now, but I'd start looking ahead. Robots are slower, but they're coming, and a dip station is exactly the kind of repeat work a machine could learn. Making the same three dips two hundred times a night is exactly the kind of work a robot could learn, so I'd start learning something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a part-time course in kitchen equipment repair, the people who fix combi ovens and dishwashers. Somebody will have to fix the robots too. I'd use AI a bit more, like for studying, and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing thunder far off when you've left washing outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why equipment repair, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the engineer, Viktor, comes in every month for our oven and he never runs out of work. He charges a fortune. If kitchens fill up with machines, someone has to keep them running, and I already know what a kitchen needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep saving. Would you cut anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I don't spend much. I share a flat with my friend Mateo, rent's fair. Maybe fewer takeaways, which is funny for a cook.

say: I'd say **front-of-house** staff like hosts and bookers mustn't be dumped.
I'd share **union posts** and ask friends' bosses for plans.
think: I'm **fine for now**, but robots are coming slowly.
My **dip station** is repeat work a machine could learn.
do: Sign up for a part-time **equipment repair** course.
Use AI more for **studying** the course.
Keep **saving** while cutting a few takeaways.
S1.quote: Making the same three dips two hundred times a night is exactly the kind of work a robot could learn, so I'd start learning something else.
fieldNote: He spots his **repeat tasks** as the weak point.
His plan is modelled on a real person: **Viktor**, the oven engineer.
He mixes **solidarity** for front staff with a personal backup plan.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time kitchen equipment repair course
Use AI to help with study notes for the course
Share union posts about protecting front-of-house staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's quick. Robots in 2031, I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a government plan right now: training money, wage support, a tax on the robots to pay for it. I'd go to the union meeting and say the same thing. Workers didn't ask for this and shouldn't pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried. In 2028 the thinking AI arrives, and that hits Samir's ordering and the office first, and maybe fewer people go out to eat because they lose office jobs. Then in 2031 the robots arrive for me. Three years between the thinking AI and the robots is just enough time to learn to fix machines, if I start the day the news breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the repair course straight away, full time if I could, living off my savings for a year. I'd ask Viktor if I could shadow him on Mondays, my day off. And I'd stop putting money into the fund and keep it as cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but I'm not sure it's a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd live on savings for a year. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about. Nine months saved, plus what's in the fund. If I picked up weekend shifts at Cedar House while studying, it works. Tight, but it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if repair work gets automated too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm back where I started, I know. But a robot fixing a broken robot in a greasy kitchen seems a long way off. That's my bet anyway.

say: I'd call for a **robot tax** to fund training and wages.
I'd tell the union **workers shouldn't pay** for this.
think: **Fewer diners** after 2028 could hit Cedar House first.
The **2031 robots** would then reach my cold section station.
do: Start the **repair course** full time, living off savings.
Move fund money into **cash** to stay flexible.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan he isn't sure about.
S2.quote: Three years between the thinking AI and the robots is just enough time to learn to fix machines, if I start the day the news breaks.
fieldNote: He sees an **indirect hit**: office job losses mean fewer diners.
His **savings** make a full-time retraining year possible.
He admits his **repair bet** could also fail.

steps.text: Study kitchen equipment repair full time on savings
Shadow Viktor, the oven engineer, on Mondays
Push the union to back a robot tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels more like a plan than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things about a robot tax, but I'd also say this is a chance to fix the training system. Five years is enough for colleges to teach robot repair properly if the government pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay, honestly. With five years' warning I can train properly while still cooking at my restaurant, instead of jumping with my eyes shut. By 2034, when the robots arrive in kitchens, I'd want to be the person installing them, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the repair course part time over two years, keep cooking at Cedar House, and then try to get an apprenticeship with an engineering firm. I'd keep saving and investing like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful. There's time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel to install the machine that replaces someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. Maybe I'd feel like a traitor. But someone will do it, and I'd rather it's someone who knows what cooks go through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Samir about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight. He'd laugh at first, then he'd probably ask me to fix the dishwasher for free.

say: I'd push for colleges to teach **robot repair**.
I'd still back a **robot tax** to pay for it.
think: Five years means I can train **without panic**.
I'd rather **install** the robots than be replaced by them.
do: Take the **repair course** part time over two years.
Apply for an **engineering apprenticeship** after the course.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more **hopeful** with time to plan.
S3.quote: With five years' warning I can train properly while still cooking at my restaurant, instead of jumping with my eyes shut.
fieldNote: Time turns his plan from a **gamble** into a calm route.
He admits feeling like a **traitor** installing robots.
His **politics** stay focused on public training money.

steps.text: Take the repair course part time over two years
Apply for an engineering apprenticeship around 2029
Keep monthly payments into his index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be forty when it really hits the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone being left behind with ten years' notice. It'd be a failure of politics if cooks end up on the street in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd probably stay a cook longer, try to become a proper chef de partie, which means running a section, and switch around 2035. Ten years is long enough that I could become a proper chef first and still switch to fixing machines before any robot needs my station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, the knife course and maybe the repair course in the evenings, slowly. Keep the fund going. I'd make a proper decision about switching once the thinking AI shows up in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Ten years is a long time for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'm not the type to wait forever. If friends start losing office jobs to AI, I'll move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything else in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd buy a place with my savings in a few years. A small flat, nothing fancy. Then at least my rent can't go up when everything else changes.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** to leave cooks behind.
I'd call any 2039 job losses a **failure of politics**.
think: I'd stay a cook and aim for **chef de partie** first.
do: Take the **repair course** slowly in the evenings.
Look at buying a **small flat** in a few years.
feel: Mostly **calm** with ten years of runway.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I could become a proper chef first and still switch to fixing machines before any robot needs my station.
fieldNote: Long warning lets him put **cooking ambition** first.
His trigger to move is **friends losing office jobs**.
He thinks about **owning a home** as protection from rising costs.

steps.text: Work towards running a section at Cedar House
Take the repair course slowly in the evenings
Save towards buying a small flat in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of the thinking AI, because of what comes three years after it. Restaurants only exist because people have money to spend, so if AI takes office jobs, my restaurant feels it before any robot arrives. What would help is cheap or free training in repair trades, and some wage support while you study, so people don't have to burn all their savings like I would.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the customers. Everyone forgets that if people lose office jobs, they stop eating out. That could hurt us before any robot does.

headlineQuote: Restaurants only exist because people have money to spend, so if AI takes office jobs, my restaurant feels it before any robot arrives.
portrait: Bilal is a **junior cold-section cook** at Cedar House, a busy Lebanese restaurant.
He has **nine months saved** plus an index fund, and lives with a friend.
He backs a **robot tax** and public training, and uses AI now and then.
His escape route is **equipment repair**, modelled on the oven engineer Viktor.
He goes from **calm** with no change to **anxious** with two years' warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because **robots** would reach kitchens just **three years** later.
whatWouldHelp: Free **repair training** with **wage support** while studying.
